title: Government Tells Supreme Court Detention Response Ready, Needs Fine-Tuning
excerpt: The Centre sought until 15 October to file its affidavit answering petitions alleging illegal detentions and transport shutdowns during Delhi's anti-CEC protests on 10 October. The Solicitor General said the draft was final but should be more comprehensive.
body:
• The Union government told the Supreme Court on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, that its response to petitions alleging illegal detentions and transport shutdowns in Delhi on 10 October is ready but needs more fine-tuning.
  • A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant gave the government until Thursday, 15 October, to file its reply affidavit, and asked that it be shared by 14 October if possible.
  • Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the affidavit was final but he wanted to make it more comprehensive, according to The Hindu.
  • Petitioners — including media organisations and lawyers' groups — allege unlawful detention, forcible removal and assault of journalists and protesters, and seek a full list of everyone detained on 10 and 11 October.

The Union government told the Supreme Court on Tuesday that its response to petitions alleging illegal detentions and a shutdown of public and rail transport, including Metro services, in Delhi on 10 October is ready but needs more fine-tuning. The court extended the deadline for the government's reply, setting up a fuller hearing later this week on how the capital was policed during protests against the Chief Election Commissioner and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

What the government said, and where

The statement was made in the Supreme Court, before a three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, The Hindu reported. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, said he had gone through the prepared affidavit, that it was final, but that he wanted to make it more comprehensive.

https://x.com/ashokdadhwal196/status/2109802648191091064

The Bench extended the time for the government to file the reply affidavit by Thursday, 15 October. On the petitioners' request, the court asked Mehta to share the affidavit, if possible, by 14 October, so that petitioners' lawyers could be prepared and the Thursday hearing would be meaningful, The Hindu reported.

Multiple petitions, including ones seeking contempt proceedings, were adjourned to 15 October, as one of the judges on the Bench was unwell, and the Bench rose for the day shortly afterwards, according to the same report.

On the source's account, the fine-tuning is a final affidavit the Solicitor General wants to make more comprehensive before filing. Its contents were not reported by The Hindu.

The allegations the affidavit must answer

The petitions arise from police action around the anti-CEC and SIR protests on 10 and 11 October. Separate petitions by media organisations, including the Free Speech Collective and the Network of Women in Media, India, allege that violence against journalists on both days was not isolated obstruction but a course of police action comprising unlawful detention, forcible removal, physical assault, manhandling, intimidation and disregard of press credentials, The Hindu reported. Those are the petitioners' allegations, not court findings.

The court also agreed to urgently hear fresh petitions seeking an independent probe and contempt proceedings over continued police action against journalists, especially women media professionals, covering the protests despite an apex court order on 11 October, according to The Hindu. Chief Justice Kant asked the petitioners to cure defects so the pleas could also be taken up on 15 October.

Another petition, by the Lawyers' Association for Constitution, alleged police brutality against detained people and sought a complete list of everyone detained on 10 and 11 October, with time, place, grounds, officers responsible and custody details, The Hindu reported.

Context: the earlier court directions

The Tuesday hearing follows a special Sunday sitting at which the Supreme Court directed that there should be no detention except in accordance with procedure established by law, that Metro and rail facilities should function normally unless restrictions were justified on public-order grounds, that barricades should be reviewed, and that internet facilities should remain undisturbed as per law, Bar and Bench reported. In that hearing, petitioners' lawyers sought contempt action; the Solicitor General said most detained people had been released the same day and Metro operations had not been curtailed — competing accounts the affidavit is expected to address.

Senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia also mentioned an incident on 12 October, when opposition leaders came to the court registry after filing a petition seeking a probe into the SIR and allegations against the CEC, and the petition complained of a stampede-like situation and sloganeering inside the premises, The Hindu reported.

What happens next

All eyes are on two dates in the court's own timetable: sharing of the affidavit by 14 October, if possible, and the comprehensive hearing on 15 October, when the detention petitions, contempt pleas and fresh journalist petitions are listed together. Until it is filed and tested, the government's substantive defence has not been set out in the reporting read for this article.
